title: Apply biological and chemical control of alien invader plants

lessons.title: Health and safety for chemical control
lessons.html:
Why alien invader control matters

Alien invasive plants such as wattle, pine, gum, lantana and triffid weed use large amounts of water, push out indigenous plants and grazing, increase fire intensity and block rivers. Landowners have a legal duty to control listed invasive species under the National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Act 10 of 2004 and its Alien and Invasive Species Regulations, and under the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983.

Hazards in chemical control

  • Herbicide exposure through skin, eyes, breathing spray mist, or swallowing
  • Contamination of rivers and boreholes, which harms aquatic life and people downstream
  • Drift onto crops, gardens and indigenous plants
  • Cuts from chainsaws, brushcutters and bush knives used in cut-stump work
  • Falling trees, uneven ground, snakes, bees, heat stress

Safety practices

AreaWhat to do
Before workRead the herbicide label and safety data sheet; know first aid steps for that product; check PPE and equipment
PPEAs the label states, typically chemical-resistant gloves, overalls, boots, eye protection or face shield; chainsaw PPE (chaps, helmet, visor, hearing protection) for felling
MixingMix away from water, in a bunded or level area, upwind; use measuring jugs kept only for chemicals
ApplyingDo not spray in wind or before rain; keep the buffer distance from water that the label requires; use only products registered for use near water when working in riparian zones
HygieneNo eating, drinking or smoking while working; wash hands and face before breaks; wash overalls separately

Emergencies

If herbicide gets on skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash with plenty of water. If in the eyes, rinse with clean running water for several minutes. If swallowed or if someone feels ill, take them and the product label to a clinic or doctor and call the poison information line. Report all incidents to the supervisor. Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993 the employer must train workers and provide PPE, and workers must use it.

lessons.title: Identifying alien invaders and indigenous replacements
lessons.html:
Know your target

Correct identification prevents spraying the wrong plant and helps choose the right control method. Learn the invaders common in your region from field guides, the local Working for Water team or extension officers.

Common problem invaders in South Africa

Woody trees and shrubsShrubs, herbs and cactiWater weeds
Black wattle, silver wattle, green wattleLantanaWater hyacinth
Port Jackson willow, rooikransTriffid weed (Chromolaena)Parrot's feather
Long-leaved wattleBugweedWater lettuce
PinesPom-pom weedRed water fern
Eucalyptus (gum) speciesFamine weed (Parthenium)Spanish reed (Arundo)
Mesquite (Prosopis)Prickly pear, jointed cactus
HakeaQueen of the night cactus
Syringa, jacaranda, poplarInkberry, mother-of-millions
Sesbania (red sesbania)Castor oil plant

Use the plant's leaves, flowers, pods, bark and growth form to identify it. Take a sample or photo to your supervisor when unsure. Some invaders, like Parthenium, can cause skin and breathing allergies, so wear gloves and avoid handling bare-handed.

Replacing aliens with indigenous plants

Cleared land invites re-invasion unless it is covered quickly. Indigenous species suited to the local area and veld type should be encouraged or planted. Examples include:

  • Sweet thorn (Vachellia karroo) in drier areas
  • Wild olive (Olea europaea subsp. africana)
  • Karee and other Searsia species
  • River bushwillow (Combretum erythrophyllum) along rivers
  • White stinkwood (Celtis africana)
  • Tree fuchsia (Halleria lucida)
  • Sand olive (Dodonaea viscosa)
  • Sagewood (Buddleja saligna)
  • Indigenous grasses to stabilise soil after clearing

Choose species with the help of a local nursery or botanist so they match the rainfall, soil and frost of your area.

lessons.title: Biological control and types of herbicides
lessons.html:
Biological control

Biological control uses natural enemies, usually insects, mites or fungi, from the invader's country of origin, to weaken it. Agents are released in South Africa only after years of testing by researchers such as the Agricultural Research Council to make sure they attack only the target plant.

InvaderExample agents
Prickly pearCactus moth (Cactoblastis) and cochineal insects
Water hyacinthWeevils (Neochetina) and others
Port Jackson willowGall-forming rust fungus
Long-leaved wattleBud-galling wasp and seed-feeding weevil
Hakea, red sesbania, lantanaSeveral seed- and leaf-feeding insects

Your role in biological control

  • Collect agents from established sites or receive them from the programme as instructed.
  • Release them on healthy, actively growing target plants, in sites protected from herbicide spraying and fire.
  • Mark and record release sites with GPS coordinates and dates.
  • Do not spray or burn release sites; it kills the agents.
  • Monitor and report agent establishment and damage.

Biological control is slow but long-lasting and cheap. It is most effective combined with mechanical and chemical control in an integrated plan.

Types of herbicides

Only herbicides registered under Act 36 of 1947 for the target species and method may be used. They can be grouped by:

  • Selectivity: selective herbicides kill some plant types (for example broadleaves) but not others (grasses); non-selective ones kill most plants.
  • Action: systemic herbicides move inside the plant to the roots, important for re-sprouting woody plants; contact herbicides kill only the parts they touch.
  • Formulation: water-based, oil-based for bark application, granules for soil application.
  • Use near water: some products are registered for use in or near water; most are not.

Your supervisor chooses the product. Your job is to apply it exactly as the label says.

lessons.title: Preparing and applying herbicide
lessons.html:
Choosing the method

MethodUsed for
Foliar spraySeedlings, low shrubs, coppice regrowth; spray leaves until wet but not dripping
Cut stumpFelled trees: cut low and level, apply herbicide to the cut surface straight away, especially the outer ring (cambium)
Basal barkThin-barked young stems: apply oil-based mix around the lower stem
Frill or stem injectionLarge standing trees: axe cuts around the trunk, herbicide into the cuts
Hand pullingSmall seedlings in moist soil, no chemical needed

Preparing the solution

  1. Read the label for the rate for your target species and method.
  2. Wear the label PPE.
  3. Half-fill the knapsack or container with clean water.
  4. Measure the herbicide accurately with a measuring jug. Never guess.
  5. Add it to the water, then top up to the final volume.
  6. Add dye if your team uses it, so you can see which stumps or plants are treated.
  7. Close the container and mix well. Label it.
  8. Triple-rinse the measuring jug and pour rinse water into the tank.

Mix only what you will use that day. Never mix near a river, dam or borehole.

Applying

  • Check the weather: no wind that causes drift and no rain expected soon.
  • Apply as soon as possible after cutting for cut-stump treatment; the surface dries and seals.
  • Cover every stump and target plant. Missed stumps coppice and must be treated again later.
  • Keep the label buffer from water and from crops.
  • Do not spray indigenous plants.

After application

  • Rinse equipment away from water and apply rinse water to the treated area.
  • Store chemicals locked away; handle empty containers as the label says.
  • Record: date, site, species, method, product, volume used and team.
  • Return to treat regrowth and seedlings in follow-up rounds.

Key points

  • Use PPE, keep chemicals away from water, and know first aid for the product.
  • Identify the invader correctly and plan indigenous replacement.
  • Protect biocontrol release sites from spraying and fire.
  • Use only registered herbicides at the label rate and the right method.
  • Treat cut stumps immediately and do follow-up rounds.
